title: Four Packets of Papad and a Borrowed Rs 80 on a Girgaum Terrace
dek: In March 1959 seven Bombay housewives started making papads with borrowed money and a rule never to accept donations.

story.founder: Jaswantiben Jamnadas Popat, Parvatiben Ramdas Thodani, Ujamben Narandas Kundalia, Banuben N. Tanna, Laguben Amritlal Gokani, Jayaben V. Vithalani and Diwaliben Lukka
story.company: Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad
story.event: Seven women start making papads on a Bombay terrace with a borrowed Rs 80 and a no-donations rule
story.summary: On 15 March 1959 seven Gujarati women in Girgaum, Bombay, among them Jaswantiben Jamnadas Popat, made four packets of papad on a terrace using Rs 80 borrowed with the help of social worker Chhaganlal Karamsi Parekh. Advised by him to keep accounts, hold high standards and never accept donations, they ran it as a business; first-year sales were Rs 6,196. The cooperative, owned by its women members, had more than 40,000 members in 62 branches by 2002 and still refused donations.
paragraphs: On 15 March 1959 seven women from Lohana Niwas, a cluster of five residential buildings in Girgaum, in South Bombay, met on a terrace and made four packets of papad. They were Gujarati housewives from families of modest means. "We were semi-literate which restricted our chances to get jobs," Jaswantiben Jamnadas Popat, one of the seven, told the BBC fifty years later. But they knew how to make papad, and a little money of their own would ease the load on their husbands.

They had no capital at all. With the help of a social worker, Chhaganlal Karamsi Parekh, they borrowed Rs 80 and bought urad flour, asafoetida and black pepper. They rolled the papads, dried them on the terrace and took them to a shop nearby; Popat recalled in 2021 that they sold quickly and the shopkeeper asked for all they could make. Parekh, whom they called Chhaganbapa, told them to keep daily accounts and to hold to high standards at any cost. Popat said he "advised us that if we wanted to experience success, never accept donations." They chose to run it as a business, taking profit and bearing loss, not as a charity. Papads that fell below standard were given away locally rather than sold.

Sales in the first year came to Rs 6,196. Word spread through neighbours and a local newspaper. By the BBC's account 25 women had joined within three months, and within three years there were about 300, so members began taking dough home to roll. In 1966 the group registered as a society, which opened the way to low-interest bank loans.

The rule outlasted the poverty it was made in. By 2002 Lijjat had more than 40,000 member-owners in 62 branches and annual sales above Rs 3 billion, and it still refused donations; after the Gujarat earthquake of January 2001 its branches gave more than Rs 4.8 million to relief. When Popat was named for the Padma Shri in January 2021, she was still living in a small room in Lohana Niwas.

quote.text: Now I am clearly of opinion that a man should live by right and by authority, and not either by recompense or favour. How many gallant men have rather chosen to lose their lives than to be debtors for them?
quote.translator: Charles Cotton (1685), ed. W. C. Hazlitt
quote.source_title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne — Complete, tr. Charles Cotton, Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
quote.connection: Montaigne wanted to live by right rather than by favour, and the sisters' rule against donations says much the same. Yet the cooperative began on a borrowed Rs 80 and a mentor's advice, and Popat was still paying tribute to him fifty years on. Its independence rested on one debt chosen with care.

reflection: The sisters' rule was not pride for its own sake. A gift would have left them grateful; a loan and a shopkeeper's order left them accountable, to customers and to each other. Even so, they did not begin alone. Someone lent them the Rs 80 and told them to write the accounts up every day.

You may be weighing help of your own just now, from a grant, a relative or a friend with money or time to spare. Montaigne would ask what each kind leaves you owing. That question is worth answering before you say yes, and it is reasonable to take some kinds of help and turn others down.
invitation: Think of one offer of help you are considering. Write a single line on what it would leave you owing, and to whom, then make no decision about it today.

research_notes: Where the first papads were sold: Popat (Gujarati Mid-day, 2021) says a nearby grocery shop; WIPO says a local merchant; the English Wikipedia article says a merchant in Bhuleshwar. The story says 'a shop nearby'. Early growth: the BBC and WIPO say 25 members within three months, Popat in 2021 said about 25 by the end of the first year and about 300 within two years, and the World Bank case says 7 to 300 in the first three years; the story attributes the three-month figure to the BBC and uses 'within three years'. The cooperative's name has two accounts (a contest with a Rs 5 prize, per Wikipedia; a choice from the next day's newspaper horoscope letter, proposed by an older member, Dhirajben, per Popat in 2021), so the naming is left out. Registration: WIPO and Popat give 1966; Wikipedia gives July 1966 for registration and September 1966 for KVIC recognition; the story says only that it registered in 1966. Popat's age is given inconsistently (80 in the BBC in 2009, 93 in Mid-day in 2021, 94 in The Better India) and is not used; a Wikipedia mirror gives a death date in 2023 that was not confirmed, so the story makes no claim about her now. Scale figures are taken from the World Bank case for 2002; the BBC gave 45,000 members and a turnover of nearly $100m in 2009, and Mid-day an annual turnover of Rs 1,800 crore in 2021. The founders' names follow the English Wikipedia list and Mid-day (which spells Banuben as Bhanuben). The Gujarati Mid-day interview was read in Gujarati and is paraphrased, not quoted. The Lijjat website's opening paragraph describes the weather on 15 March 1959; that detail is not used. Montaigne's line comes from 'Of Vanity', where he writes of preferring to live by legal right rather than by the favour of powerful neighbours; it is applied here by analogy.
